title: 2025-06-18-verdigris-surge-governance-and-kms-pathways
summary: Intro/discovery on Reserved GPU capacity, tenant fencing, burst model and KMS/encryption integration. Customer evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private for latency-sensitive inference; priority on isolation and auditability. Agreement to run a short benchmark and share security whitepaper and pricing bands.
topics: Burst strategy and fallback to hosted
transcript:
[00:00] Samira: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Samira from Redwood. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Evelyn: Evelyn Park here, CTO at Verdigris.
[00:10] Ravi: Ravi Patel, head of Platform.
[00:12] Priya: Priya Shah, security.
[00:15] Diego: Diego Flores, Redwood SE.
[00:18] Samira: Awesome. Goal for today is to understand your surge patterns and requirements for reserved capacity and surface any security gating items. Roughly 45 minutes. Sound good?
[00:29] Evelyn: Yup, sounds great. To give context, we're moving an embedding/search + chat assistant into production. Currently on a mix of self-hosted models and API calls. We need predictability for peak times, and can't have noisy noisy neighbors during certain windows.
[00:48] Leo: Also we have PII and some regulated datasets so key residency and auditability are top concerns.
[00:55] Samira: Got it. Can you walk through traffic profile? average qps, spikes?
[01:01] Ravi: Baseline is about 40 qps for generation endpoints, embeddings around 10 qps. Spikes 4x during marketing pushes, and occasionally a 10x flash we saw in Feb for a product launch. Those spikes last between 3-30 minutes. We want a pre-warm/hotpool to handle bursts without cold-start latency.
[01:25] Diego: Are those bursts predictable by cron or are they ad-hoc?
[01:28] Ravi: Mostly ad-hoc but with some scheduled campaigns. We need both automated burst scaling and a guaranteed reserved floor for steady throughput.
[01:36] Samira: Redwood Dedicated supports reserved GPU pools + burst capacity. We do warm-pools that pre-provision KV caches and can route to a hosted fallback if Dedicated capacity is exhausted. For isolation we offer tenant fencing, dedicated nodes, and strict VLAN/VPC segmentation on Private.
[02:00] Priya: Quick question — KMS. We need to ensure keys never leave our control; can Redwood integrate with our KMS/HSM?
[02:07] Diego: Yes, we support customer-managed KMS via Cloud KMS or external HSM integrations in Private deployments; for Dedicated we can support VPC + customer KMS in some configs. We'll have the security docs.
[02:20] Priya: Is there envelope encryption or is it server-side only?
[02:24] Maya: We can do envelope encryption and provide audit trails for key usage. I'll follow up with the exact architecture diagram.
[02:32] Evelyn: Good. Regarding isolation: we want to avoid warm-pool co-tenancy with other customers during high risk windows. Can we pin physical nodes?
[02:41] Diego: Yes — Dedicated can be single-tenant racks or fully private on-prem. You can choose reserved nodes with tenant-only allocation or shared pools with strict cgroup limits. There's a cost tradeoff though.
[02:52] Ravi: What are common patterns — do customers reserve just enough for baseline and rely on hosted for spikes, or reserve big enough to avoid fallback?
[02:59] Samira: Both patterns are common. Many SaaS teams reserve baseline capacity and set policy-based burst to hosted or higher-cost reserved pools. Others with strict latency or compliance reserve the bulk. We can run a cost/lambda-style projection based on your qps + model choices.
[03:18] Evelyn: On models — we'll likely use a mix of open LLMs for embeddings and a tuned chat model for gen. How does your compile/runtime handle quantized models and long-context KV cache? Latency is critical.
[03:30] Diego: Our serving runtime picks kernels based on model architecture and sequence lengths; kv cache prewarm helps reduce token latency. Quantized runtimes are supported — we'll share our perf matrix. In practice you can often 2-3x throughput with INT8 quantization at minor quality cost.
[03:45] Leo: Any limitations with batch sizes when running low-latency flows?
[03:49] Diego: Continuous batching is workload-aware; we enforce latency SLOs and will avoid large batching for low-latency routes. You can configure per-route SLOs.
[03:58] Priya: On compliance, we need SOC2 + ISO and a full audit trail for prompts and responses, retention controls, and redaction options.
[04:06] Samira: We provide audit logs, per-token retention settings, and redaction tooling; SOC2 is a standard ask — we can share certs and our compliance pack.
[04:16] Ravi: For a pilot, what's a sensible reserved commit? Say we want to cover baseline and a 3x burst cushion for a week-long campaign.
[04:25] Diego: We'd size GPUs based on model throughput — for instance a single A10G-ish slot is approx X gen qps for chats, Y for embeddings; I'll run a sizing estimate after we get payload stats. Practically many customers start with 8-16 GPUs reserved for a pilot.
[04:43] Samira: Let's capture tech and business constraints so we can propose two options: performance-first (larger reserved, single-tenant) and cost-first (baseline reserve + hosted fallback).
[04:53] Evelyn: Sounds good. Also curious about failover runbooks — if your Dedicated region loses capacity mid-spike, how do we failover without losing consistency?
[05:01] Diego: We have multi-region routing and automatic fallback to hosted variants. For session consistency we replicate KV caches within region zones; for strict consistency you'd want cross-region replication, which adds latency. We'll document tradeoffs.
[05:14] Ravi: We need an SLA for max token latency p99 and also a billing protection if fallback to hosted increases unit cost.
[05:22] Samira: We can discuss contractual SLAs in the proposal and include egress/overage protections for pilot.
[05:28] Priya: One more on network: do you support private peering or direct connect for Dedicated?
[05:33] Maya: Yes, VPC peering and direct connect are available for Dedicated and Private. For on-prem we do an air-gapped packaging option.
[05:41] Evelyn: Excellent. Any performance benchmarks we can run?
[05:44] Diego: We propose a short 72-hour bench: 1) steady-state baseline qps 2) synthetic flash bursts at 5x/10x for 5-20 minutes 3) cold-start and warm-pool latency. We'll run it on a representative model you pick.
[06:00] Leo: We'll need to anonymize payloads. Also want to evaluate key-rotation behavior while the bench runs.
[06:06] Samira: Totally. We'll provide a bench plan and a data handling NDA addendum if needed.
[06:12] Evelyn: Ok great. On commercial side, how are reserved commits structured? monthly/annual? credits?
[06:18] Samira: Dedicated is typically monthly or annual reserved capacity with tiered pricing for single-tenant vs shared pools. There's also burst credits and an overage policy. I'll include pricing bands in the follow-up.
[06:29] Ravi: Competitors — we're also talking to Anthropic and a couple of infra vendors. How do you present cost comparisons?
[06:36] Jordan: We can produce a unit-cost per token + per-embedding projection across models and include latency curves. We also show real customer telemetry for similar topologies.
[06:46] Evelyn: Ok, let's talk next steps.
[06:48] Samira: Recap: Redwood to share security whitepaper and SOC2 docs, bench plan, preliminary sizing estimate, and pricing bands. Verdigris to share anonymized request traces and a list of critical SLOs. We'll sync in a week.
[07:02] Priya: Action for us — I'll assemble traces and a security checklist.
[07:06] Samira: Great. Anything else?
[07:08] Ravi: Not from me. Thanks.
[07:10] Samira: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with a calendar invite for the bench kickoff and send the docs.
[07:16] (call ends)

Note: Transcript contains occasional transcription errors and speaker overlap; timestamps are approximate.
